propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision dismissing their appeal of RPD decision denying refugee status due to viable IFA.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board, dated September 30, 2019, dismissing their appeal of a decision by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] under which they were denied the status of refugees or persons in need of protection, as defined by sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], because they have a viable Internal Flight Alternative [IFA].

paragraphs.summary: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision dismissing their appeal of RPD decision denying refugee status due to viable IFA, court states.

propositions.text: Applicants are married Bangladeshi citizens fearing persecution for different reasons.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are a married couple and citizens of Bangladesh. The Applicants both claim fearing persecution in Bangladesh but for different reasons.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant fears Awami League and Jubo League; other Applicant fears Hefazat-e-Islam.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant, Md Abdul Hannan, fears the Awami League and the Jubo League. The other Applicant, Ferdous Afsana, fears Hefazat-e-Islam.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants are married Bangladeshi citizens fearing persecution for different reasons, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. Hannan refused to issue letter of credit in 2015, was pressured and assaulted by Jubo League members.
propositions.quote: Mr. Hannan’s claim is related to a conflict, which arose when he refused to issue a letter of credit to a client of the bank where he was employed in 2015. As a consequence, he was pressured and assaulted by members of the Jubo League, the youth wing of the Awami League.

propositions.text: He filed police complaint and received calls urging withdrawal and contributions to Jubo League.
propositions.quote: Following the assault, the Principal Applicant filed a complaint with the police. Thereafter, he received calls urging him to withdraw his complaint and contribute funds to the Jubo League.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. Hannan refused letter of credit, was assaulted by Jubo League, filed police complaint, then received calls urging withdrawal and contributions, court states.

propositions.text: Police took Mr. Hannan from home on Feb 17, 2016, advising to issue letter or pay league.
propositions.quote: On February 17, 2016, several police officers took the Principal Applicant from his home and advised him to either issue the letter of credit or make a payment to the league.

propositions.text: Mr. Hannan took leave two months later and traveled to friend's residence in Chittagong in April 2016, arriving Canada June 4, 2016.
propositions.quote: Mr. Hannan requested a leave from his employer two months after these events and travelled to a friend’s residence in Chittagong in April 2016. He arrived in Canada on June 4, 2016.

paragraphs.summary: Police took Mr. Hannan from home advising letter or payment; he took leave, traveled to Chittagong, then arrived in Canada, court states.

propositions.text: Ms. Afsana was low-level activist in Gonojagoron Moncha, assaulted by Hefazat-e-Islam in Dec 2015.
propositions.quote: Ms. Afsana was a low-level activist within Gonojagoron Moncha, a protest movement in Bangladesh. In December 2015, she was allegedly assaulted when confronted by members of Hefazat-e-Islam, an Islamist group.

propositions.text: She filed police complaint, was pressured to withdraw it, kidnapped by group for nearly 4 months starting April 11, 2016.
propositions.quote: She filed a complaint with the police. Thereafter, Ms. Afsana was allegedly pressured by the group to withdraw the complaint. On April 11, 2016, she was allegedly kidnapped by the group and held for nearly 4 months.

propositions.text: Mr. Hannan filed missing person report when wife disappeared.
propositions.quote: Mr. Hannan filed a missing person report when his wife disappeared.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Afsana was activist assaulted, pressured to withdraw complaint, kidnapped for nearly 4 months; Mr. Hannan filed missing person report, court states.

propositions.text: Ms. Afsana escaped hospital in August 2016, entered Canada August 31, 2016; Applicants filed refugee claims shortly after.
propositions.quote: In August 2016, Ms. Afsana found herself in a hospital and was able to escape. She entered Canada on August 31, 2016. The Applicants filed refugee claims shortly thereafter.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Afsana escaped hospital, entered Canada August 31, 2016; Applicants filed refugee claims shortly after, court states.

propositions.text: RPD found Mr. Hannan's testimony generally credible but found Ms. Afsana not truthful on central claim aspects.
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Principal Applicant’s testimony was, generally, credible. However, the RPD concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, Ms. Afsana was not being truthful about central aspects of her claim, specifically her alleged encounters with Hefazat‑e‑Islam.

propositions.text: Ms. Afsana testified she would not join any political party if returned to Bangladesh.
propositions.quote: She testified that should she return to Bangladesh she would not become involved in any political party.

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Mr. Hannan credible but Ms. Afsana not truthful on key claims; she said she would avoid political involvement if returned, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: RPD found Applicants had viable IFA in Chittagong and thus were not refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD determined that the Applicants had a viable IFA in Chittagong. Therefore, it held that they were not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection

paragraphs.summary: RPD found Applicants had viable IFA in Chittagong and denied refugee status, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: RAD agreed Ms. Afsana was not kidnapped by Hefazat-e-Islam; Applicants did not request RAD hearing on credibility but submitted new documents under IRPA s.110(4).
propositions.quote: The RAD agreed with the RPD that Ms. Afsana had not been kidnapped by Hefazat‑e‑Islam. The Applicants did not request a hearing before the RAD with regard to the issue of credibility but submitted new documents pursuant to section 110 (4) of IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: RAD agreed Ms. Afsana was not kidnapped; Applicants submitted new documents but did not request RAD hearing on credibility, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: RAD found first three new documents were pre-RPD decision and readily available; no reasonable explanation for late submission; did not accept them.
propositions.quote: The RAD held that the first three items referred to information, which arose prior to the RPD rendering its decision and were readily available to the Applicants prior to the decision. The RAD found that the Applicants had provided no reasonable explanation for their failure to provide this information prior to the RPD rendering its decision and did not accept them.

propositions.text: Letter from mother post-dated RPD decision but provided no new information; given no weight by RAD.
propositions.quote: While the letter from the mother post-dated the RPD decision, it did not provide any new information and was given no weight.

paragraphs.summary: RAD rejected new documents as pre-RPD and unexplained late; letter from mother post-dated RPD but added no new info, given no weight, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: RAD found Principal Applicant faced no serious persecution risk in Chittagong; Ms. Afsana would face no risk if not politically involved.
propositions.quote: The RAD found that the Principal Applicant faced no risk of serious persecution in Chittagong. Considering that Ms. Afsana would no longer be involved in any political party, the RAD found that Ms. Afsana would also face no risk of serious persecution in Chittagong.

propositions.text: RAD confirmed RPD decision; Applicants not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: Therefore, the RAD confirmed the RPD’s decision and concluded that the Applicants were not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: RAD found no serious persecution risk in Chittagong for Applicants, confirmed RPD decision denying refugee status, earlier decision-maker found.

propositions.text: Applicants assert they received negligent or incompetent assistance from immigration consultant during claim processing.
propositions.quote: On this application, the Applicants assert that they had received negligent or incompetent assistance of counsel from the consultant.

propositions.text: Applicants were represented by immigration consultant; a bar member appeared for RPD hearing.
propositions.quote: In the processing of their claims, the Applicants were represented by an immigration consultant although a member of the bar appeared on their behalf for the RPD hearing.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants assert negligent assistance from immigration consultant; court notes consultant representation and bar member at RPD hearing.

propositions.text: Issues: Was Applicants' counsel negligent or incompetent? If so, was it determinative? Is RAD decision reasonable?
propositions.quote: The issues in this proceeding are as follows: Was the Applicants’ counsel negligent or incompetent? If so, was the counsel’s negligence or incompetence determinative? Is the RAD’s decision reasonable?

paragraphs.summary: Court states issues: counsel negligence, its determinative effect, and reasonableness of RAD decision.

propositions.text: IRPA ss.96-97 define Convention refugee and person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The following legislative provisions of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 are relevant to this judicial review: Convention refugee Définition de réfugié 96 A Convention refugee is a person who, by reason of a well-founded fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group or political opinion, 96 A qualité de réfugié au sens de la Convention — le réfugié — la personne qui, craignant avec raison d’être persécutée du fait de sa race, de sa religion, de sa nationalité, de son appartenance à un groupe social ou de ses opinions politiques : (a) is outside each of their countries of nationality and is unable or, by reason of that fear, unwilling to avail themselves of the protection of each of those countries; or a) soit se trouve hors de tout pays dont elle a la nationalité et ne peut ou, du fait de cette crainte, ne veut se réclamer de la protection de chacun de ces pays; […] […] Person in need of protection Personne à protéger 97 (1) A person in need of protection is a person in Canada whose removal to their country or countries of nationality or, if they do not have a country of nationality, their country of former habitual residence, would subject them personally 97 (1) A qualité de personne à protéger la personne qui se trouve au Canada et serait personnellement, par son renvoi vers tout pays dont elle a la nationalité ou, si elle n’a pas de nationalité, dans lequel elle avait sa résidence habituelle, exposée : (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or a) soit au risque, s’il y a des motifs sérieux de le croire, d’être soumise à la torture au sens de l’article premier de la Convention contre la torture; (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if b) soit à une menace à sa vie ou au risque de traitements ou peines cruels et inusités dans le cas suivant : (i) the person is unable or, because of that risk, unwilling to avail themself of the protection of that country, (i) elle ne peut ou, de ce fait, ne veut se réclamer de la protection de ce pays, (ii) the risk would be faced by the person in every part of that country and is not faced generally by other individuals in or from that country, (ii) elle y est exposée en tout lieu de ce pays alors que d’autres personnes originaires de ce pays ou qui s’y trouvent ne le sont généralement pas, (iii) the risk is not inherent or incidental to lawful sanctions, unless imposed in disregard of accepted international standards, and (iii) la menace ou le risque ne résulte pas de sanctions légitimes — sauf celles infligées au mépris des normes internationales — et inhérents à celles-ci ou occasionnés par elles, (iv) the risk is not caused by the inability of that country to provide adequate health or medical care. (iv) la menace ou le risque ne résulte pas de l’incapacité du pays de fournir des so

paragraphs.summary: Court cites IRPA ss.96-97 defining Convention refugee and person in need of protection, prior authority states.

propositions.text: Vavilov establishes reasonableness as presumptive standard for judicial review, with exceptions not applicable here.
propositions.quote: As determined by the Supreme Court of Canada in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 30, reasonableness is the presumptive standard for most categories of questions on judicial review, a presumption that avoids undue interference with the administrative decision maker’s discharge of its functions. While there are circumstances in which the presumption can be set aside, as discussed in Vavilov, none of them arise in the present case.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Vavilov: reasonableness is presumptive standard for judicial review; exceptions not applicable here.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review focuses on actual decision and justification, not on court's own view or new analysis.
propositions.quote: The court conducting a reasonableness review must focus on the decision the administrative decision maker actually made, including the justification offered for it. A court applying the reasonableness standard does not ask what decision it would have made in place of the administrative decision maker, attempt to ascertain the range of possible conclusions, conduct a new analysis or seek to determine the correct solution to the problem. Instead, the reviewing court must consider only whether the decision made by the decision maker, including both the rationale for the decision and the outcome to which it led, was unreasonable (Vavilov at para 83). VI. Analysis A. Was the Applicants’ counsel negligent or incompetent?

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Vavilov: reasonableness review focuses on actual decision and justification, not court's own view or new analysis.

propositions.text: Applicants argue counsel failed to disclose decisive employment evidence, leading to negative credibility finding upheld by RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that Ms. Afsana’s appeal before the RAD was dismissed because her former counsel failed to disclose decisive evidence to the RPD that was in his possession and pertained to her employment with the bank, namely an employment letter, an employee ID card, and a business card. They argue that her employment at the bank was central to her kidnapping allegations and that her failure to produce proof of employment led the RPD to make a negative credibility finding that was upheld by the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue counsel failed to disclose employment evidence, causing negative credibility finding upheld by RAD.

propositions.text: Negligence allegations against counsel must be specific, supported by evidence, per Jeffrey v Canada and Federal Court protocol.
propositions.quote: Allegations of negligence against former counsel must be sufficiently specific and clearly supported by evidence: Jeffrey v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 605 at para 9. They must also satisfy the Federal Court’s protocol on allegations against counsel or other authorized representatives in citizenship and immigration cases.

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Jeffrey and protocol: negligence allegations against counsel must be specific and supported by evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants' present counsel gave notice to former counsel per protocol; correspondence is part of record.
propositions.quote: In accordance with the protocol, Applicants’ present counsel gave notice of the allegation of incompetence or negligence to the former counsel. Their resulting exchange of correspondence forms part of the record in these proceedings.

propositions.text: Applicants acknowledge they must prove incompetence without hindsight and that outcome would differ but for incompetence.
propositions.quote: The Applicants acknowledge that they must establish that former counsel’s acts or omissions constituted incompetence without relying on hindsight and that the outcome would have been different but for the incompetence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' counsel gave notice to former counsel; Applicants acknowledge burden to prove incompetence without hindsight and causation.

propositions.text: Former counsel said employment proof was provided before RAD appeal, supported by mailed envelope copy.
propositions.quote: The former counsel was asked if he had received proof of employment from Ms. Afsana before the RPD proceedings were concluded. The former counsel responded that it was provided to him in preparation for the appeal to the RAD and provided a copy of an envelope mailed from Bangladesh in support of that assertion.

propositions.text: Envelope appears to contain letter from Principal Applicant’s mother, not bank employment records.
propositions.quote: However, this appears to have contained the letter from the Principal Applicant’s mother rather than the bank employment records.

paragraphs.summary: Former counsel said employment proof was provided before RAD appeal, but envelope contained mother's letter, not employment records, court finds.

propositions.text: Former counsel was negligent for not advising to provide documents before RPD and not explaining to RAD why not submitted earlier
propositions.quote: The Applicants contend that the former counsel was negligent when he failed to advise them to provide these documents before the RPD proceedings and failed to explain to the RAD why they were not previously submitted.

propositions.text: Proof of Ms. Afsana’s employment was determinative and would have supported her kidnapping claim
propositions.quote: They argue that the issue was determinative as proof of Ms. Afsana’s employment would have supported her claim to have been kidnapped.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue former counsel was negligent for not submitting documents earlier and that proof of employment was determinative for kidnapping claim.

propositions.text: At RPD hearing, Ms. Afsana said employment proof could be obtained if necessary, implying she did not have it then
propositions.quote: At the RPD hearing, Ms. Afsana had been asked whether she had any proof of employment. She responded that such evidence could be obtained if it was necessary, thus suggesting that she did not have it in her possession at that time.

propositions.text: Former counsel disputed claim that documents were provided before RPD; said they were received after RPD decision and submitted to RAD
propositions.quote: Her claim to have provided the documents before the RPD hearing was disputed by the former counsel. He claims that they were received subsequent to issuance of the RPD decision and put forward to the RAD on the appeal, in response to the RPD’s credibility findings.

paragraphs.summary: At RPD, Ms. Afsana said employment proof could be obtained if needed; former counsel disputed earlier submission, said documents came after RPD decision.

propositions.text: Conflict exists between Applicants' and former counsel's evidence but no need to resolve it
propositions.quote: there is a conflict between the evidence of the Applicants and that of their former counsel. It is a conflict that I do not consider necessary to resolve

propositions.text: Applicants failed to show substantial prejudice from former counsel’s alleged inaction
propositions.quote: the Applicants have failed to demonstrate that substantial prejudice flowed from their former counsel’s alleged inaction.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds conflict between Applicants and former counsel but no need to resolve; Applicants failed to show substantial prejudice from counsel's inaction.

propositions.text: Present counsel's inquiries about failure to present documents and negligence claim have some merit
propositions.quote: The Applicants’ present counsel were correct to make inquiries about the failure to present the documents during the RPD proceedings and their submissions about the former counsel’s negligence in failing to obtain the employment documents for the purpose of those proceedings have some merit.

propositions.text: Documents' relevance to Ms. Afsana’s claim is dubious; they show earlier employment, not at relevant time
propositions.quote: the relevance of the documents to the basis of Ms. Afsana’s claim is dubious. They do not establish employment at the bank at the relevant time, but rather earlier.

propositions.text: Ms. Afsana claimed harassment and kidnapping due to political involvement, not employment
propositions.quote: she said she was harassed, abused, and kidnapped because of her involvement in a political organization not because of her employment.

propositions.text: Conflict between her claim and objective evidence about Islamist group’s kidnapping practices was main reason she was not believed
propositions.quote: the conflict between her claim and the objective documentary evidence about the kidnapping practices of the Islamist group was the primary reason why she was not believed.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants' present counsel's negligence claim has merit but documents are irrelevant; harassment claim based on politics, not employment; credibility issue was main reason for disbelief.

propositions.text: Determinative issue was viability of internal flight alternative (IFA) in Chittagong
propositions.quote: The determinative issue in the case at hand was the viability of an IFA in Chittagong.

propositions.text: RAD found Ms. Afsana would be safe in Chittagong as she no longer intends political involvement
propositions.quote: the RAD found that she would be safe in Chittagong because she no longer intends to be involved with any political party.

propositions.text: Proof of employment was irrelevant to RAD’s IFA finding
propositions.quote: Her proof of employment was irrelevant to this finding.

propositions.text: RPD’s credibility finding based on implausibilities and inconsistencies with objective evidence
propositions.quote: The RPD’s credibility finding was based on a number of implausibilities in Ms. Afsana’s testimony and inconsistencies with the objective documentary evidence.

propositions.text: RAD did not base decision on credibility
propositions.quote: the RAD did not base its decision on credibility.

propositions.text: Former counsel’s omission had no impact on proceeding outcome
propositions.quote: previous counsel’s alleged omission had no impact on the outcome of the proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds IFA viability was key; RAD found Ms. Afsana safe in Chittagong; employment proof irrelevant; RAD decision not based on credibility; counsel omission had no impact.

propositions.text: Applicants say RAD’s IFA findings are speculative and ignored contradictory evidence including a letter from friend in Chittagong
propositions.quote: The Applicants submit that the RAD’s IFA findings are speculative and that the RAD ignored important contradictory evidence, notably a letter from the Principal Applicant’s friend with whom he had sought shelter in Chittagong before coming to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD’s IFA findings are speculative and ignored contradictory evidence including a letter from friend in Chittagong.

propositions.text: To find viable IFA, tribunal must be satisfied on balance of probabilities no serious persecution risk exists there
propositions.quote: When determining the existence of a viable IFA, the tribunal must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the applicant being persecuted in the part of the country to which an IFA exists.

propositions.text: Tribunal must also consider all circumstances, including claimant’s, to decide if it’s reasonable to seek refuge in IFA
propositions.quote: The tribunal must also determine that, in all of the circumstances, including the circumstances particular to the claimant, conditions in the part of the country where a potential IFA has been identified are such that it would not be unreasonable for the applicant to seek refuge there

propositions.text: Cites Rasaratnam and Ohwofasa cases on IFA test
propositions.quote: Rasaratnam v Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 FC 706 at 711; Ohwofasa v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 266 at para 19.

paragraphs.summary: Law requires tribunal to find no serious persecution risk and reasonableness of refuge in IFA, citing Rasaratnam and Ohwofasa.

propositions.text: Applicants claim inquirers about friend’s home in Chittagong were Jubo League members
propositions.quote: The Applicants claim that the persons who had inquired about the new occupant of the friend’s home in Chittagong while Mr. Hannan was residing there were members of the Jubo League.

propositions.text: Inquirers did not identify as Jubo League members nor ask for Principal Applicant by name
propositions.quote: However, the persons inquiring had not identified themselves as members of the Jubo League nor asked for the Principal Applicant by name.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant acknowledged in RPD hearing that inquiries were because he was a stranger
propositions.quote: During the RPD hearing, the Principal Applicant appeared to acknowledge that the people in Chittagong inquired about him because he was a stranger.

propositions.text: RPD and RAD concluded no evidence that inquirers were Jubo League or seeking Principal Applicant
propositions.quote: Both the RPD and the RAD concluded that there was no evidence that the people inquiring about the Principal Applicant were from Jubo League or that they were looking for the Principal Applicant.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants claim inquirers were Jubo League; RPD and RAD found no evidence they were or sought Principal Applicant; he acknowledged inquiries were due to being a stranger.

propositions.text: NDP shows Jubo League has nationwide presence and was involved in conflict in Chittagong
propositions.quote: The National Documentation Package [NDP] indicates that the League has a nationwide presence and had been involved in a conflict in Chittagong between its parent organization, the Awami League and the main opposition party, the BNP.

propositions.text: This conflict is irrelevant to claims in these proceedings
propositions.quote: This long-standing and ongoing conflict is irrelevant to the claims at issue in these proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: NDP shows Jubo League’s nationwide presence and conflict in Chittagong, but court finds conflict irrelevant to these claims.

propositions.text: RAD assessed evidence and gave it appropriate weight
propositions.quote: The RAD assessed the evidence and gave it the weight it considered appropriate.

propositions.text: RAD concluded Principal Applicant failed to reasonably explain why he would be persecuted in Chittagong
propositions.quote: The RAD concluded that the Principal Applicant had failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why he believes that he would be persecuted in Chittagong.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably concluded no serious risk of persecution in Chittagong for Principal Applicant or Ms. Afsana
propositions.quote: As a result, the RAD reasonably concluded that the Principal Applicant faced no serious risk of persecution in that IFA and there was no basis for concluding that Ms. Afsana would either.

paragraphs.summary: RAD weighed evidence, found Principal Applicant failed to explain persecution risk, and reasonably concluded no serious risk for him or Ms. Afsana in Chittagong.

propositions.text: Record does not support that former counsel’s incompetence caused substantial prejudice to Applicants’ RAD appeal
propositions.quote: The record before the Court does not support a conclusion that the alleged incompetence or negligence of the Applicants’ former counsel resulted in substantial prejudice to their appeal before the RAD.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes record does not support that former counsel’s incompetence caused substantial prejudice to Applicants’ appeal.

propositions.text: RAD’s determination of internal flight alternative in Chittagong was reasonable; no basis to overturn
propositions.quote: The RAD’s determination that the Applicants have an internal flight alternative in Chittagong was reasonable and there is no basis for this Court to overturn that decision.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD’s internal flight alternative determination reasonable and declines to overturn it.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance proposed; none certified; application dismissed
propositions.quote: No serious questions of general importance were proposed, and none will be certified. JUDGMENT IN IMM-6396-19 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that the application is dismissed. No questions are certified.

paragraphs.summary: Court dismisses application, finds no serious questions of general importance, and certifies none.
